title: A Little Girl Gave Me Her LAST Dollar in 1991. 31 Years Later...

scenes.text: Sweetheart, on a December night in nineteen ninety-one, I was stranded at a bus stop in Mansfield with no purse, no money, and no way home. And a little girl about seven, in a coat two sizes too big, walked over and pressed a dollar bill into my hand. Her only dollar. Her Christmas money. I gave her something back that night. And thirty-one years later, I saw it again, pinned to a nurse's uniform.
scenes.query: little girl giving dollar at snowy bus stop
scenes.caption: HER ONLY DOLLAR

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you what I gave that little girl, and the night in a hospital room in two thousand twenty-two, when I was seventy-eight and very sick, and a nurse leaned over my bed and said six words I'll never forget. Stay with me, honey.
scenes.query: hospital room at night soft light
scenes.caption: SIX WORDS

scenes.text: It was the Friday before Christmas, honey. I'd gone downtown after work to buy Harold's present, a new wristwatch, and I'd spent the afternoon in the stores on Main Street. And somewhere between the jewelry counter and the parking lot, my purse was stolen right off my shoulder. Wallet, car keys, everything. And when I got to my car, I couldn't get in. It was dark, and it was eleven degrees.
scenes.query: dark parking lot downtown at night winter
scenes.caption: ELEVEN DEGREES

scenes.text: This was before cell phones, sweetheart. I didn't have a quarter for the pay phone. I went back to the stores, but they were closing. So I walked to the bus stop on Fourth Street, thinking I could beg the driver to let me on. The sign said, exact fare, one dollar. And when the bus came, the driver shook his head and said, sorry, ma'am. Rules. And he drove away. The next bus wasn't for an hour.
scenes.query: city bus pulling away from snowy stop
scenes.caption: EXACT FARE ONE DOLLAR

scenes.text: I sat down on that cold bench, forty-seven years old, and I'm not ashamed to tell you I cried. My feet were numb. My hands were numb. And across the street, there was a little laundromat with the lights on, and inside I could see a young mother folding clothes, and a little girl sitting on the washing machine, watching me through the window. In a minute I'll tell you what that little girl did.
scenes.query: laundromat window at night with child watching
scenes.caption: WATCHING ME

scenes.text: She came out the door and crossed that street by herself, honey, in a man's winter coat that came down past her knees, with the sleeves rolled up four times. Tennis shoes, no boots, in the snow. Her nose was running. She walked right up to me and said, lady, why are you crying? And I said, oh, honey, somebody took my purse, and I can't get home.
scenes.query: little girl in oversized coat crossing street
scenes.caption: WHY ARE YOU CRYING?

scenes.text: And she reached into the pocket of that big coat and pulled out a dollar bill. It was folded up very small, into a little square, the way children fold money they're saving. And she said, here. You can take the bus. And I said, oh, sweetheart, no. That's your money. And she said, it's my Christmas money for my mom. But you need it more. She's not crying.
scenes.query: child's hand holding folded dollar bill
scenes.caption: SHE'S NOT CRYING

scenes.text: If Grandma's story is touching your heart, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. I looked across the street, and her mother was standing in the laundromat doorway, watching, with her arms crossed against the cold. And she nodded at me. Just once. Go ahead. That mother didn't have much, honey. You could see it. But she let her daughter give it anyway.
scenes.query: young mother in laundromat doorway nodding
scenes.caption: SHE NODDED

scenes.text: I took that dollar, sweetheart. I took it because she needed me to take it. You can't refuse a gift like that. But I wanted to give her something back, and I had nothing. No purse, no money. Then I felt it, on the lapel of my coat. A little silver angel pin, with a tiny blue stone in the middle. My mother had given it to me the Christmas before she died.
scenes.query: small silver angel pin with blue stone
scenes.caption: THE SILVER ANGEL

scenes.text: My mother had passed in nineteen eighty-nine, honey, just two years before. And that pin was the last gift she ever gave me. I'd worn it every day since. And I took it off my coat and pinned it on that little girl's enormous coat, right over her heart. And I said, this is a guardian angel. She watched over me. Now she's going to watch over you. What's your name, honey?
scenes.query: pinning angel on little girl's coat
scenes.caption: SHE'LL WATCH OVER YOU

scenes.text: She said, Tasha. And then the bus came, and I had to go. I got on with her dollar, and I sat at the window, and I watched that little girl standing at the bus stop in her giant coat, touching the angel pin with one finger, until the bus turned the corner. I told Harold the whole story that night. He held me while I cried. And then he said, Ruthie, you'll see her again.
scenes.query: woman on bus looking back through window
scenes.caption: YOU'LL SEE HER AGAIN

scenes.text: When I got home that night, Harold had to break a basement window to let us in, because my house keys were in the stolen purse too. He didn't care one bit. He wrapped me in the afghan off the couch, made me a cup of cocoa, and sat my numb feet in a pan of warm water. And while I told him about Tasha, I watched his face. I'll tell you what my Harold did the next morning in a minute.
scenes.query: woman wrapped in afghan with feet in water pan
scenes.caption: BROKE A WINDOW

scenes.text: He drove downtown first thing and talked to the bus company, honey. He told them the whole story, and he asked them, from now on, to let anybody ride free on Christmas week who couldn't pay. They said no. Rules. So every December after that, for seventeen years, until he passed, Harold left a roll of dollar bills with the drivers at the Fourth Street depot, for whoever came up short. He never told anybody but me.
scenes.query: man handing money to bus driver at depot
scenes.caption: A ROLL OF DOLLARS

scenes.text: I went back to that laundromat, honey, the very next Saturday, with a box of groceries and a Christmas present for Tasha. A real winter coat, in her size, and red boots. But the woman at the counter said the young mother and her girl only came in once in a while, and she didn't know their names or where they lived. I left the box with her. I don't know if they ever got it. I went back four more times. I never saw them again.
scenes.query: elderly woman in laundromat holding gift box
scenes.caption: I NEVER SAW THEM AGAIN

scenes.text: So far, the stolen purse, the bus that wouldn't wait, a little girl's folded dollar, and my mother's silver angel. I kept that dollar, sweetheart. I never spent it. I put it in a little frame, and it hung in my kitchen for thirty years, right next to the calendar. Every time I looked at it, I said a little prayer for Tasha, wherever she was. Stay with me, because then I got sick.
scenes.query: framed folded dollar bill on kitchen wall
scenes.caption: I NEVER SPENT IT

scenes.text: In February of two thousand twenty-two, I got pneumonia, honey. Bad. I was seventy-eight, and my lungs were full, and they took me to the hospital in an ambulance in the middle of the night. Susan flew in from Arizona. Mark slept in a chair by my bed. For three days, the doctors weren't sure I was going to make it. I don't remember much of those three days.
scenes.query: ambulance at night in snow
scenes.caption: THEY WEREN'T SURE

scenes.text: But I remember the fourth night. I woke up at two in the morning, and the room was dark, and I was scared. And a nurse came in to check my oxygen. A tall woman, about thirty-eight, with her hair in braids and the kindest, calmest voice. She held my hand and said, Miss Ruth, you're doing better. Your numbers are good. And I looked up at her, honey, and on her blue scrubs, right over her heart, there was a little silver angel with a blue stone.
scenes.query: nurse at bedside at night hospital room
scenes.caption: A SILVER ANGEL

scenes.text: I couldn't talk very well, because of the oxygen mask. But I reached up with my hand, and I touched that pin. And she looked down at it, and she smiled, and she said, oh, this? Somebody gave this to me when I was a little girl. A lady at a bus stop. And I pulled the mask down, and I said, Tasha? And she froze, sweetheart. She just froze.
scenes.query: elderly patient touching pin on nurse's scrubs
scenes.caption: TASHA?

scenes.text: She looked at my chart. Ruth. She looked at my face, for a long time. And then she said six words. She said, I prayed I'd find you. And she sat down on the edge of my bed, at two in the morning, and we both cried so hard that the other nurse came running to see if my monitors were broken.
scenes.query: nurse and elderly patient crying together
scenes.caption: I PRAYED I'D FIND YOU

scenes.text: Tasha told me everything over the next week, honey, on her breaks. Her mother had been raising her alone, working two jobs, and they'd been living in a shelter that winter. That's why they used the laundromat. They moved to Akron in the new year, before they ever got my box. And her mother had told her, every Christmas after that, that angel pin means somebody believed in you. Don't you ever forget it.
scenes.query: young mother and daughter in shelter room 1990s
scenes.caption: SOMEBODY BELIEVED IN YOU

scenes.text: She'd worn that pin on her coat all through grade school, sweetheart, and on her dress at her high school graduation, the first in her family. She wore it under her gown when she got her nursing degree. And she'd pinned it on her scrubs every single shift for twelve years. She said, every scared patient I hold hands with at two in the morning, I'm thinking about the lady at the bus stop.
scenes.query: nursing school graduation young woman
scenes.caption: EVERY SINGLE SHIFT

scenes.text: When I went home from the hospital, Tasha came to my house on Maple Drive and saw her dollar bill, still folded in its little square, in the frame by my calendar. Thirty-one years. She put her hand on the glass. And she said, Miss Ruth, you never spent it. I said, honey, how could I? It was the most valuable dollar anybody ever gave me. It got me home.
scenes.query: nurse touching framed dollar on kitchen wall
scenes.caption: IT GOT ME HOME

scenes.text: Tasha and her mother came to Christmas dinner that year, sweetheart. Her mother, Denise, is about my daughter's age, and the two of them talked all night. Tasha has a little girl of her own now, eight years old. And on Christmas Eve last year, Tasha took the angel pin off her own scrubs and pinned it on her daughter's coat. And she told her the whole story. The bus stop, the dollar, and the lady who cried.
scenes.query: mother pinning angel on daughter's coat Christmas
scenes.caption: PASSED ON AGAIN

scenes.text: Here's what I want you to remember, honey. There's no such thing as a small kindness. A dollar, a pin, a hand to hold at two in the morning. You never know where it's going to land. Tell me in the comments, sweetheart, has a child ever done something kind for you that you never forgot? There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: silver angel pin on child's red coat
scenes.caption: NO SMALL KINDNESS
